story_text.value:
At my previous company, I spent hours every month going through our bank statements and looking for the invoice behind each charge.

There are many invoice collectors, with varying accuracy, but AI makes this much better now. I also noticed that while checking the statements, I was subconsciously reviewing the tools we pay for.

So I built a free tool that works exactly how I wanted it to. It combines invoice collection with spotting forgotten subscriptions and duplicates, alerts for price rises and renewals, and some nifty actions, like drafting an email to ask for a discount. Many times it works, you just need to ask.

It's fully free, but limited to reading 100 invoices a month, since I cover the AI costs and make no money from it.

I also want to release a self-hosted version, where you could use your own models, including local ones. The code needs some cleanup and refactoring first, so I'll do it if people actually use this (I set the goal at 100 users).

title.value: Show HN: Free tool to collect invoices and spot forgotten subscriptions

story_text.value:
Hi HN! After we launched our public beta, some of our ex-colleagues tested the approach of creating decision models based on their work artefacts and noticed that it led to fewer back-and-forth cycles to clarify details and greater productivity in their daily routine.

The market for professionals has a downside: the problem of scaling the business model. You physically can't have more hours in a day, and as a professional, you manage the flow of incoming clients through pricing and balancing your personal time.

The AI market has a downside: the problem of model subjectivity. You can set boundaries through "prompt engineering" and say, "Respond as a professional." But after a couple of messages, you'll ask something like, "...maybe doing it this way would be better?" and the model will agree with you. Because the model doesn't have its own point of view.

We're solving this problem by creating an expert's decision model. Then another user who needs that expert's expertise can ask it questions and get answers about how the expert would act in that case.

From a technical perspective, we initially used a RAG architecture to build expert models. However, this approach (uploading all the artifacts and trying to create a replacement or copy of an expertise) turned out to be a failure.

So we took a completely different approach, similar to how you would compare movies from different genres. This led to a significant improvement in the quality of answers.

title.value: Show HN: Avva – Compress your expertise available to AI agent via MCP

story_text.value:
Hi HN,

One day I built a native "Outloud Reader" application for IOS and Android devices that reads any photo page, PDF or text out aloud in a natural voice and highlighting each phrase in karaoke style. This application could be helpful for any student or language learner.

Idea of this application was born when my wife told me that it would be great to have an application that could turn any book page into audio so she could listen to it while walking or driving. She also needs it to practice her listening skills while studying english and read texts that teacher gives them as homework.

I know there are many such applications that could read any text out loud but most of them just read the text without highlighting each phrase or cost too much. so, inspired by the idea, I decided to create my own application that will have everything my wife needs.

I spent a lot of time trying to find the way how to make it work and not pay all the money I have. I spent a lot of time to find any TTS open-source models and I found something that works and has everything I need for my idea. Now the application sends pages to my server where LLM recognizes the text and translates it if needed and then voice it with this model. The next big challenge for me was to make it work as karaoke and highlight text synchronously with the audio and I found the best model for that - "whisper" that really helped to bring this idea to life.

Now it can do the following: - voice any text, pdf or photo in 14 languages with a natural voices - highlight every phrase like in karaoke - translate any page into the language you're learning - generate stories with AI and turn it into audio - work offline that allow to listen to it in any place - sync generated audio between devices

So after a few months of hard work on it as a pet project, "Outloud Reader" raised to the best application that really helps my wife to improve her listening skills and even more, gave me a lot of experience in building such projects.

Any feedback, bugs or ideas are very welcome!

story_text.value:
I am Luc, one of the co-founders of Lightscale AI. I have background in programming languages (ETH Zurich) and we are small team in Zug, Switzerland. As more and more code is now written by LLMs and few people have time to review the generated code, we came up with the idea to revise the actual stack below the LLMs: The programming language with its compiler and runtime system, all designed from scratch for AI authorship, not for humans.

We have three goals: 1. Security and stability by language design: Some classes of errors are removed by abstraction as the AI never writes that code, but the compiler and runtime implement it fully. Others are reduced by rigid compiler checks and very strict language rules (no fun for humans to code). 2. Speed. We designed the language to reduce tokens, by throwing out a lot of complexity and legacy of classical languages. Our target is about a minute from prompt to deployment on average. 3. AI cost. The language is designed for mid-tier LLMs, with little or no reasoning effort. This is why we can offer prompting for free (no credit, but account sign-up is needed). We charge for longer hosting or source export.

For now, we focus on business application, but plan to extend the approach to general-purpose software. Longer write-up: https://lightscale.ai/articles/why-llms-need-their-own-progr...

Happy to hear your feedback.

title.value: Show HN: Lightscale AI – A language for LLMs to write business software

story_text.value:
137 file types; a single file with nothing to install. Introducing Provost, the free compression and archival tool that can create 119 formats, and open 137 total. It's new custom format packs smaller than ZPAQ, xz, and Zstandard in tests. JPEG, PNG, PDF, DOCX/XLSX, and gzip are unpacked and repacked for ~25% smaller files; ability to encrypt to people's keys or a password; can open archives straight from HTTPS, S3, WebDAV, and SFTP; can search inside archives, including the text of Office files and PDFs; and much more.

Q&A --- Is it open source? It is not.

Will my .provost files open in five years? I've committed to future releases reading every 0.1.0 archive, and to old compression methods staying readable.

Are builds signed? No. The Mac app isn't notarized and the Windows exes are unsigned, so you will see Gatekeeper and SmartScreen warnings.

Is the .exe an installer? Nope; it's a stand-alone executable. This is true for all GUI and CLI builds across all three OSes.

Is the custom .provost compression fast? Levels 7 to 9 are very slow. There is a built-in benchmark test.

How was it built? AI.

story_text.value:
Especially as I've been using AI and churning through an order of magnitude more software on my computer, I've been wondering what best practices are to stay abreast of compromises, bad releases, hacked software, etc. I've been wondering what a reasonable duration of lagging behind updates is to allow for exploited software to be alerted by the community, while also updating quick enough that I don't let my system remain with known + fixed bugs. I anticipate the answer is partly: use less software, containerize/sandbox, and understand what I install. But that's not fun, not always possible for the multitude of applications I actually use to intentionally interface with my sensitive data, and not always possible due to time constraints.

What have you guys been doing to hedge against corrupted software? Anyone have any leads on where I could read deep dives from experts on this topic?

title.value: How to Stay Abreast of Compromised Software?

hits.author: grapemane
hits.story_text:
Especially as I've been using AI and churning through an order of magnitude more software on my computer, I've been wondering what best practices are to stay abreast of compromises, bad releases, hacked software, etc. I've been wondering what a reasonable duration of lagging behind updates is to allow for exploited software to be alerted by the community, while also updating quick enough that I don't let my system remain with known + fixed bugs. I anticipate the answer is partly: use less software, containerize/sandbox, and understand what I install. But that's not fun, not always possible for the multitude of applications I actually use to intentionally interface with my sensitive data, and not always possible due to time constraints.

What have you guys been doing to hedge against corrupted software? Anyone have any leads on where I could read deep dives from experts on this topic?
hits.title: How to Stay Abreast of Compromised Software?
